paras: The threatened lynching of Ed Partridge followed the death of his six-year-old stepdaughter, Bell Holmes, on a Georgia plantation near Americus in late October or early November 1881. A coroner's jury found that the girl died of beatings at Partridge's hands, and he escaped from custody before a New York wire dispatch reported that local citizens threatened to lynch him. No lynching or recapture appears in the coverage, which spread the case nationally as a brief item under headlines such as "A Georgia Brute."

According to the Americus Republican, as quoted by the Savannah Morning News, Partridge was "a bright negro man" of about 21 or 22 who had lived that year on the place of Judge H. H. Singleton with his wife, a child, and his stepdaughter. The Republican wrote that Singleton knew of Partridge's "cruel nature" and had heard of his beating the girl.

On a Monday around noon, Partridge told Singleton that Bell was dead, gave a workman her measure for a coffin, and left to have a grave dug. Suspicious because he had not heard the child was sick, Singleton examined the body, sent a courier for Coroner J. E. Phelps, and issued a warrant that Constable E. M. Jones served that night. Partridge was held with a trace chain looped around his neck and fastened to a tenant house, but on Tuesday morning, while no one was in the house, he twisted the chain apart with a wagon hammer and fled.

That morning the coroner empaneled a jury, and Dr. R. T. Bivins reported the body covered with sores, with skin and flesh slipped off in several places. After hearing several witnesses, the jury found that Bell Holmes died "from cruel treatment in the way of beating with sticks, switches, ropes and such, in the hands of Ed. Partridge."

A special dispatch dated Americus, November 10, reported that "the citizens threaten to lynch him," and the South Branch Intelligencer added that he "was committed to jail, but escaped." The coverage does not report Partridge's recapture, any mob action against him, or a trial.

The fullest account came from the local Americus Republican, which the Savannah Morning News reprinted on November 8 as "a horrible tragedy," detailing the injuries and the inquest without mentioning any threat of lynching. A separate Georgia item, run in Savannah on November 9 and in the Marietta Journal on November 17, described a "small negro girl" whipped to death by her "brutal step-father in Schley county." The Washington National Republican's "Doings in Dixie" column, copied by the Bolivar Bulletin in Tennessee, likewise named "Edward Partridge, a Schley County (Ga.) negro."

Outside Georgia, the case was known mainly through a two-sentence New York special that the Richmond Dispatch printed under "Whipped to Death" and the National Republican under "A Georgia Brute," both on November 11. That dispatch identified Partridge as "colored," stated as fact that he had whipped the girl to death, and added that "the flesh was beaten from the body." Over the next two weeks it was copied, often word for word, in news-brief columns of papers such as the Daily Republican, the Centre Democrat, the Cambria Freeman and the Clarke Courier, the Knoxville Daily Chronicle attributing it to Augusta rather than Americus.

The wire dispatch said Partridge whipped the girl to death "yesterday," or November 9, but the Republican's account was already in print in Savannah on November 8 and described the Tuesday inquest, and the November 9 Georgia item placed the death "last week," so the local report points to a date around October 31. The wire placed the case at Americus, while the Georgia state-news items located it in Schley County; the local account names only Judge Singleton's place.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Ed Partridge
bases: The reported violence was the beating death of a six-year-old girl attributed to her stepfather; the only collective element was a wire line that 'the citizens threaten to lynch him' after he had escaped, with no mob action reported (A1, A3, A4).

No one was reported killed by a mob: Partridge escaped from a constable's chain before any threat was reported, and the dispatch says only that citizens threatened to lynch him over the child's death (A1, A3, A12).

The Americus Republican's account (A1), the Schley County state-news item (A2, A7) and the Americus wire dispatch (A3, A4, A6) independently report the child's death and name Partridge, though the lynching threat appears only in the wire dispatch.

framing.detail: Northern and Southern dailies and weeklies printed the two-sentence dispatch in news-brief columns, the National Republican headlining it 'A Georgia Brute'.
The Americus Republican's account, reprinted in Savannah, called the case 'a horrible tragedy' and dwelt on the injuries and the inquest, saying nothing of mob threats.

info: Partridge reported the girl dead on a Monday ('last Monday') before Nov. 8, 1881, and the coroner held the inquest the next day; the Nov. 9 Savannah item placed the death 'last week'. The wire dispatch dated Nov. 10 said 'yesterday' (Nov. 9) and some reprints said 'on Wednesday'.
On Judge H. H. Singleton's place, where Partridge had lived that year; the dispatch was datelined Americus, Ga. (one version says Augusta).
Ed. (Edward) Partridge, 'colored', about 21 or 22, threatened with lynching; the child who died was his stepdaughter Bell (Belle) Holmes, about six, described as a 'small negro girl'.
Accused of beating his stepdaughter to death; a coroner's jury found she died 'from cruel treatment' by beating 'in the hands of Ed. Partridge'.
'The citizens', unnamed and of unstated number, were said to threaten to lynch Partridge.
0 by a mob; the child, described as Black, died of a beating attributed to her stepfather.
Partridge was at large after his escape; no report of his recapture, a lynching or a trial was found.
